items.gist: The passage introduces the ordered classification of tattvas, beginning from Shiva as one and proceeding through the manifested levels.
It states that bodies and worlds raise no difficulty and presents the cause-effect relation as posited by Shiva's will.
Only Shiva, the independent Lord, is the true agent; dependent inert things cannot possess agency.
The text rejects the idea that inert entities such as seed and sprout can stand in genuine causal succession.

items.topic: Shiva alone agent; causal order as appearance
items.gist: It concludes that Shiva alone is agent and explains causal order as ordered appearance rather than inherent necessity.

items.topic: Yogi's will, dream, and firm cause-effect
items.gist: Causal regularity appears through yogi's will and dream-like ordered perception, while true causality belongs to consciousness.
Aggregate causes are discussed, and Shiva alone acts independently in joining and separating instrumental causes.
Shiva is the universal agent, and even human sense of agency is ultimately Shiva's action.
The wonderful character of cause-effect in world and scripture is illustrated through examples such as scorpions arising from dung.
The tattva order from purusha upward is set out, with niyati and related principles arranged according to the Matanga teaching.
Shiva's five powers are divided fivefold, yielding five tattvas and five groups of mantras.

items.topic: Critique of separate tattvas; pure fivefold
items.gist: The passage criticizes counting Brahma and others as separate tattvas and concludes with the pure fivefold tattva whose agent is Shiva's will.
